c0324e5fcb.d:
The Phalguna Paurnami festival is a grand five-day celebration held annually at the Swami Pushkarini. Each day of the festival features a different set of deities taken for a celestial ride on a beautifully decorated float in the temple tank.

1. On the first day, Bhagavan Rama, along with Sita and Lakshmana, are worshipped and taken for a ride on the float.
2. The second day is dedicated to Bhagavan Krishna and Rukmini, who are also offered puja and taken on the float for a pleasure ride.

For the last three days, from Trayodashi to Paurnami:
1. Sri Malayappa Swami, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, are taken out for a ride in the temple tank.
2. The third day includes three rounds of the float, increasing to five rounds on the next day.
3. On the final day, the utsava murtis (festival deities) are taken for a splendid ride on the float for seven rounds, attracting a large number of pilgrims. The beauty of the deities is further enhanced by the charm of the full moon, making this day particularly special and visually stunning.

c047a872c5.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śukraḥ in viśākhā tulā, center-to-center separation 0°59′13.32″.
c047a872c5.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°59′13.32″, 0°59′03.65″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 1°53′46.91″ N, vakra (retrograde), magnitude +2.08, elongation 10°27′48.21″ W). śukraḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 0°54′33.59″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.92, elongation 10°19′53.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c05236d853.d: While the Mahalaya Paksha (typically the 5th (Dark) Paksha from āṣāḍha) is the most important time to perform pitr̥-śrāddha, our Shaastras have specified the gauṇakāla or secondary timings for the performances for these very important śrāddhas. These śrāddhas can be performed in this paksha, in case circumstances prevented the performance of the śrāddhas in the uttama-kāla. Today marks the end of the 7th (Dark) Paksha from āṣāḍha.
c05236d853.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑍌𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍋𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑍇---  
𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌯𑍋𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌃।  
𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾॥  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌿 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑍋 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈 𑌸𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌶𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍀 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌵𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌕𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌶𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾।  
𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌵𑌨𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥-𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑌿𑌃

c09ba0d081.b: Partial solar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈0.4 of 12 aṅgulas), Sun at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
c09ba0d081.d: The eclipse is already in progress at sunrise (grastodaya). Magnitude: 3% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈0.4 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 14:48►05:50 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī/hastaḥ (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or uttarāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or kr̥ttikā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: kanyā, tulā, kumbhaḥ, mithunam get more ashubha phala, makaraḥ, mīnaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, siṁhaḥ somewhat ashubha, vr̥śchikaḥ, dhanuḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
c09ba0d081.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌚॥௨௦॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌥 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।  
𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௨௧॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌚 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌘𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌮𑍇।  
𑌰𑌾𑌕𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌿 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿॥௨௨॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰 𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌃।  
𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌣𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍂𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌤 𑌏𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑌃 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾 𑌨𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍈𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌮𑍋𑌘𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌷𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌏𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍‍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌨𑍃𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௨௫॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 ௭-௧௪

c0fa71386f.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′45.25″.
c0fa71386f.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′45.25″, 0°57′40.94″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′15.14″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′19.51″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°57′00.39″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′24.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c12b453c46.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Vichara Sarman, later known as Chandesvara Nayanmar, was a prodigious child from Tiruchaijnanallur, a place renowned for Vedic learning and devotion to Bhagavan Shiva. By the age of five, he had self-learned the Vedas and Agamas due to his past life impressions. After his Upanayanam, he formally studied the Vedas under a Guru and aspired for liberation in this life.

One day, Vichara Sarman witnessed a cowherd beating a cow and intervened, admonishing the cowherd for mistreating the sacred animal. He took over the responsibility of tending the cows himself. Under his care, the cows flourished, and there was an abundance of milk, which he used to perform Abhishekam to a mud-constructed Shiva Lingam under an Atti tree (audumbaravr̥kṣaḥ) by the river.

However, a villager witnessed this and complained to the cow owners that Vichara Sarman was wasting milk on mud and sand. His father, Echhadattan, upon hearing the complaint, secretly observed Vichara Sarman's ritual. Misinterpreting his son's devotion, the father attempted to disrupt the ritual, prompting Vichara Sarman to defend the worship by striking his father with a stick, which miraculously turned into an axe and killed his father.

This act was a divine test of Vichara Sarman's devotion. Bhagavan Shiva, impressed by his unwavering devotion, appeared before him with Devi Parvati. Vichara Sarman was transformed into a divine form akin to Bhagavan Shiva and adorned with a garland from Bhagavan, attaining Saroopya Mukthi (liberation with the attainment of the form of Bhagavan). Bhagavan then declared that Vichara Sarman would soon reach Chandikeshvarar's Abode and be worshipped in the same way he had worshipped Bhagavan with food, clothes, and flowers. Both Vichara Sarman and his father, purified by this supreme act of devotion, attained the abode of Bhagavan Shiva.

c1d3e9394d.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′36.50″.
c1d3e9394d.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′36.50″, 0°18′28.67″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′01.16″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′25.13″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′37.66″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′09.45″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
c1d3e9394d.s:

c208805012.d:
On this day, a 19 year old Muslim carpenter named Ilm ud din stabbed Mahashay Rajpal on his chest eight times while he was seated in the outer verandah of his shop. Mahashay Rajpal was the publisher of rangIlA rasUl.

Context
Mahashay Rajpal Malhotra was born in a Khatri family in Amritsar on the Panchmi tithi of Ashadh Samvat (AD 1885). He came to own a publishing business. 

In 1923, Muslims published two particularly offensive books to Hindus. “Krishna teri geeta jalani padegi” used derogatory and vulgar language against Shri Krishna and other Hindu deities and “Uniseevi sadi ka maharshi” which contained derogatory remarks on Arya Samaj founder Swami Dayanand Saraswati (incidentally written by an Ahmadi). This was the time before Sec 295A was introduced in the IPC. 

To respond to this provocation, Pandit Chamupati Lal, a close friend of Mahashay Rajpal, wrote a short biography of the Islamic Prophet, Mohammed. Titled “Rangeela Rasool” this short pamphlet was a satirical take on the domestic life of Mohammed. Because of the sensitive nature of the pamphlet, Pandit Chamupati made Mahashay Rajpal promise that he would never reveal the name of the authorOn the surface, Rangeela Rasool had a laudatory tone of Mohammed’s life but at the same time pointing out uncomfortable truths about his domestic life. Though historically accurate and written after due research of hadiths, this caused an outrage among the Muslims of Lahore. 

Before the second edition could be printed, the colonial government banned the pamphlet in late June 1924. By July 1924, Muslims had filed a criminal case against Mahashay Rajpal under Sec 153A (promoting enmity between groups). During the trial, he was offered to give up the name of the real author of Rangeela Rasool and go scot-free, but he declined it and upheld his promise. In legal proceedings that lasted close to three years, in May 1927 Mahashay Rajpal was acquitted of all charges. The judge contended that Sec. 153A does not prohibit historical analysis of ‘prophets’ of different religions and if it were to be so applied, works of serious historians could also be subject to it.

Muslims all over the country went off into a frenzy. The primary organized opposition to the judgement was driven by the Khilafatists and the Ahmadis.  The British introduced 295A, criminalizing future speech deemed insulting to religious groups, passed easily in parliament with widespread support. 

In 1927, the same year he was acquitted, there were two unsuccessful attempts on his life — a wrestler named Khuda Baksh attacked him in September 1927 when he was sitting in his shop but Khatri Rajpal ji caught him and handed him over to the authorities. Khuda Baksh was convicted and sentenced to ten years in prison. The next month, a Muslim man named Aziz Ahmed attacked Swami Satyanand ji mistaking him to Khatri Rajpal. Luckily, the attack was not fatal and Swami ji recovered after a couple of months. A further attempt succeeded. 

Aftermath
As word spread among the Hindus of Lahore, a crowd of thousands gathered. Hesitant Brits gave permission for a funeral procession the next day.

Mahashay Rajpal’s killer was represented in court by Mohammad Ali Jinnah. At his funeral the poet Mohammad Iqbal, a favourite of Indian liberals today, eulogized the killer. Today his grave is a religious site in Pakistan and Pakistani textbooks eulogize him with the title of “Ghazi”.

After partition, Mahashay Rajpal’s family moved to Delhi from where “Rajpal and Sons” continues to operate today. Almost 70 years after his death, he was awarded the first “International Freedom to Publish Award” by then deputy PM LK Advani.

(source - OpIndia)

c2124495c0.d: Siṃha-Ravi-Saṅkramaṇa-Viṣṇupadī Punyakala.  For viṣṇupadī-puṇyakāla like siṁha-saṅkramaṇa, the 16 ghatikas preceding and succeeding the saṅkramaṇa form a puṇyakāla; in general, the ghatikas closer to the puṇyakāla are even more sacred.
c2124495c0.s:
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌶𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌤𑌪𑌃—  
𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍁 𑌰𑍋𑌗𑍀 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍀 𑌚 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌃 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍁 𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌆𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌕-𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 (𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌃)  
𑌷𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇।  
𑌦𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌨𑍈𑌵 𑌦𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌸𑌸𑍁𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌿𑌂𑌹𑍇 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌸𑌦𑌾॥  
---𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍌𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌭𑍇  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑌃॥  
𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌨𑌾𑌡𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌆𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌕-𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 (𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌃)

c26e7d9535.d: It is said in the Vishnu Purāṇam, that if the Amavasya of Magha month coincides with the nakashatra of Varuna, i.e. Shatabhishak, the pitr̥s are overjoyed, and do not obtain it unless they have accumulated a lot of punya! If it is Shravishtha, then the pitr̥s are satisfied for (ten) thousand years. It is said in the Smrtis, that if Amavasya falls on a Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, such a tithi is given the appellation puṣkalā and is as sacred as a solar eclipse. amāvāsyā of māgha month.
c26e7d9535.s:
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌮𑍍---

𑌋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌣 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌃 𑌸 𑌵𑌰𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌨𑍃𑌪 𑌲𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌸𑍌॥  
𑌗𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍇𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑌦𑌾 𑌨𑍁 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾 𑌮𑌘𑌾 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍂𑌯𑌃।  
𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌤𑍋𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌤𑌨𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍈𑌃॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇 𑌧𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾 𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌭𑍂𑌪𑌾𑌲 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌜𑌲𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌜𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌃॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌸𑍋𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌭𑍌𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾 𑌯𑌦𑌿।

c2acbee4d2.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°29′41.45″.
c2acbee4d2.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°29′41.45″, 0°29′21.56″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′57.16″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 3°59′23.95″ E). śukraḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°24′38.60″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 4°07′53.50″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c318736aea.d: The eclipse is still in progress at sunset (grastAstamana). Magnitude: 34% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈4.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 04:10►20:18 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

c39de5d54d.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌕𑌰𑍇।  
  
𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑍈 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍇𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌰𑍇।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑍋 𑌧𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌵𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍇  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇---  
𑌸𑌿𑌂𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍌 𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌃,  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌚𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯-𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌮𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂  
𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌊𑌰𑍍𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌨𑌿𑌷𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌃।  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇-𑌉𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍇  
𑌵𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌨𑌭𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌃 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍋 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑍇𑌦𑍍 𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇𑌯𑌃---  
𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌿 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑌶 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚 𑌚।  
𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌨𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑍀𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌲𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌯 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾।  
𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌚 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍀 𑌶𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌨𑍀॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌷𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌰𑌃।  
𑌗𑌣𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌬𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌃॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌲𑌾𑌭𑌂 𑌚 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌶𑍂𑌨 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌤𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌥𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌅𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌨 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌪𑌰𑍋 𑌨𑌰𑌃।  
𑌯𑍁𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑍋 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌵𑍈 𑌹𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌮𑌭𑍀𑌪𑍍𑌸𑌤𑌾॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍋𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌶𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌤𑍇॥  
  
𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌃।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍇।  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌚॥௨௦॥  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌥 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇।

c3a35d3130.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.97″.
c3a35d3130.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.97″, 0°10′19.15″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′02.41″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′36.18″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′36.44″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′55.89″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
c3a35d3130.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

c3a3675330.b: Observed on Śukla-Prathamā tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
c3a3675330.d: With the beginning of Chaitra māsa, it is important to give water to the needy. Therefore, it is suggested that facilities be established for distributing water. On an auspicious day, suggested by a Vipra, one should begin the ‘water pavilion’ offering. The mantra for that is translated as: “This water pavilion is dedicated to all living beings in general. By the offering of this, may the ancestors and the grandfathers indeed be satisfied.” And thereafter, water must be given for four months [continuously/without fail]. By one who is unable to offer a water pavilion, especially if they desire Dharma (virtue), a pot of water (Dharmaghata), clean, containing cool and pure water, should be given daily to the house of a Brāhmaṇa, with the mouth of the pot wrapped in cloth. The mantra for that translateas as “This Pot of Virtue is offered; it is the essence of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. By the offering of this, may all my wishes be fulfilled.” There is no doubt that the person who offers the Dharmakumbha by this prescribed method also attains the fruit of the water pavilion offering (Prapa-daana) [itself].
c3a3675330.s:
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌮𑍍𑌭 𑌉𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍇---  
𑌅𑌤𑍀𑌤𑍇 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌹𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌵𑍇।  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌰𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍।   
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃---  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌨𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌜𑌲𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌮𑍍।   
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌮𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌮𑍀𑌪𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌨𑌾॥   
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌂 𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌘𑌟𑌕𑍋 𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌨𑌃।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌯𑌃 𑌶𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌲𑌜𑌲𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌚𑌿𑌃॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌃-  
𑌏𑌷 𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌘𑌟𑍋 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌶𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌃।  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍 𑌸𑌕𑌲𑌾 𑌮𑌮 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌮𑌨𑍋𑌰𑌥𑌾𑌃॥ 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌿।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌸𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌲𑌭𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥   
---𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍌𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌭𑍇

c465acbe7c.d: Bhagavan Hayagriva did upadesha of all four Vedas to Brahma.
c465acbe7c.s:
𑌹𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍌 𑌮𑌤𑌃॥௨௧॥  
𑌹𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌜𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌅𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌹𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌵𑌃।  
𑌉𑌪𑌾𑌸𑌨𑌾𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃॥௨௨॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑍋 𑌹𑌯𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌃।  
𑌜𑌗𑍌 𑌸 𑌸𑌾𑌮𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌿𑌲𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌷𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌸𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍂𑌨𑌦𑍀𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌮𑍇।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌰𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌦𑌮𑍍॥௨௪॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌶𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌗𑌦𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌥 𑌸𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌥𑌾॥௨௫॥  
𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌡𑌿𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌜𑌨𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌹।  
𑌜𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌡𑌾 𑌚 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍀𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍃𑌲𑌬𑍍𑌧𑌯𑍇॥௨௬॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌅𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌹𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌵𑌮𑍍।   
𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌹𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍁॥௨௭॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌨𑌮𑌃 𑌶𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍇 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌥 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑍋𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍋𑌧𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௨௮॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌮𑌃 𑌶𑌬𑍍𑌦𑍋 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌦𑌶𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌰𑌃।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌷𑌟𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍈𑌕𑌸𑌾𑌧𑌕𑌃॥௨௯॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌰𑌣𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌯𑌾।  
𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌵𑌾𑌥 𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑌲𑍌 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌮𑍍॥௩௦॥  
𑌏𑌵𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍇 𑌹𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌃 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌈𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍁𑌮𑌾𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌉𑌪𑌾𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌨-𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌣𑌾𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌪𑌬𑌲𑌿𑌸𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌹𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌵𑌜𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍀𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌥𑌨𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍈𑌕𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇  
𑌓𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍀𑌥𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌾𑌯 𑌋𑌗𑍍𑌯𑌜𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌮𑌮𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇।  
𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾𑌯𑌿𑌨𑍇॥  
𑌅𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌨𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌿𑌰𑌂 𑌛𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌿 𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌶𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛 𑌮𑍇।  
𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌹𑌯𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷 𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇॥

c513e8a251.d: Pradosha Vratam. Fast during the day and perform śivapūjā in Pradosha Kala. Pradosha vratam is even more special, when if falls on a Monday, which is already a special day for śivārādhanam.
c513e8a251.s:
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑍇 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌶𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌿॥  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍋 𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌨𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑍇𑌶 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌪𑌯𑌾 𑌹𑌰॥  
  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍂 𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑍋𑌽𑌸𑌿  
𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌶𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌆𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑍌  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌹𑌲𑌂 𑌹𑌰 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑌪𑌦𑌿 𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌨𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍।  
𑌦𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌶𑌿𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌧𑌿 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇  
𑌸 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌶𑍁𑌪𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌾 𑌶𑌿𑌵 𑌪𑌾𑌵𑌨𑍀𑌤𑌿  
𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌰 𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌿 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌕𑍂𑌟𑌃।  
𑌸𑌂𑌰𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌜𑌗𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌤𑍍  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇𑌶𑌾𑌨 𑌗𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌪𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌃।  
𑌭𑌗𑍀𑌰𑌥𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌂 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍇𑌦𑌹𑍇𑌤𑌵𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌---

c51b45dbf2.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′43.49″.
c51b45dbf2.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′43.49″, 0°54′30.72″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′32.47″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°48′01.17″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′48.98″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′57.47″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c53eb55c97.d: The eclipse is still in progress at sunset (grastAstamana). Magnitude: 4% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈0.5 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 02:51►19:25 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra śravaṇaḥ/śraviṣṭhā/śatabhiṣak (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or mr̥gaśīrṣam (anujanma) or chitrā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: makaraḥ, kumbhaḥ, mithunam, tulā get more ashubha phala, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, karkaṭaḥ, kanyā, dhanuḥ somewhat ashubha, mīnaḥ, mēṣaḥ, siṁhaḥ, vr̥śchikaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

c555a59bad.d:
The Shukla-paksha Ekadashi of āśvayuja month is known as pāpāṅkuśā-ēkādaśī.

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth.

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.

𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍁𑌭𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌿॥  
  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌥𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍇 𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌵 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵।  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌵𑍈 𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑍋 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌤𑌃॥  
--𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇  
  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑍌𑌤𑌿𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈𑌕𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌵𑌯𑌃॥௧௪॥  
  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌗𑌦𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௩௫॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑍃𑌪𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮॥௩௬॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃॥௩௭॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌕𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌚𑍋𑌦𑌕𑌂 𑌪𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௩௮॥  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍀।  
𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍃𑌥𑌿𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௩௯॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍋 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃॥௪௦॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌗𑍋𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌗𑍇॥௪௧॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌃॥௪௨॥  
𑌵𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋 𑌯𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌾𑌃॥௪௩॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍈𑌰𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌭𑌮𑍍॥௪௪॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌸𑌮𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௧௮॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌶𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌉𑌮𑌾𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌵𑌧𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥௪௦॥

c56d6c5d96.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°38′09.32″.
c56d6c5d96.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°38′09.32″, 0°38′04.87″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 0°39′30.52″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.10, elongation 3°57′46.57″ W). budhaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°17′39.84″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.68, elongation 4°06′58.48″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°18′37.55″, 0°18′29.71″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°00′03.23″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.28, elongation 26°56′18.85″ E). śukraḥ at mūlā-2 dhanuḥ (latitude 1°18′40.78″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 26°57′03.19″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c5c81d0c74.d: A native of Gauḍadeśa, born in Kashmir, pious, Śrī Sureśvara, secured the knowledge of Pūrva Mīmāṁsa from Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, well-versed in Vedas, and avowed to house-holder's life; he engaged in debate with Ācārya and got initiated into asceticism. Then, attending on Ācārya, he reached the highest level in yogic practices and by the directions of the Ācārya, he lived for seventy years at the Kāma Pīṭha in Kāñci. Then, in the year 2695 of the Kali era, on the night of the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha of the Bhava year that revered Sureśa, having taken the world by surprise through his fame by traversing throughout the earth, united/merged with the Supreme Being in the path known as Laya obtained the state of beautiful form of Śivaliṅga verily in the presence of on-lookers.

c5d7f0d3c5.d: Umbral magnitude: 1.36 (parimāṇa ≈12.0 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:07►02:25 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra śatabhiṣak/pūrvaprōṣṭhapadā/uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or punarvasuḥ (anujanma) or viśākhā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: kumbhaḥ, mīnaḥ, karkaṭaḥ, vr̥śchikaḥ get more ashubha phala, mithunam, siṁhaḥ, tulā, makaraḥ somewhat ashubha, mēṣaḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, kanyā, dhanuḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

c62917bd3f.d:
On this day, Karnataka government began celebrating Obavva jayantI to honor the deeds of onake obavva of chitradurga.

Events
Onake Obavva, the wife of a common soldier, while fetching water during one of the several sieges of the fort, heard the muffled sound of enemy soldiers attempting to enter the fort walls through a small crevice that was just big enough for one person at a time to crawl through. Hiding silently next to the crevice with an onake, or pestle, she killed each soldier as his head appeared in the opening and dragged his body inside the wall. By the time her husband and others came to her aid, many dead soldiers lay around her. Onake Obavva's courage and quick thinking single-handedly saved the fort that day. 

Aftermath
Chitradurga anyway fell to Hyder Ali later. But Obavva was never forgotten. 

Her bravery is commemorated in Chitradurga by the name of Onake Obavva Stadium and by an extraordinary new sculpture near the DC Office. In 2021, Karnataka government started celebrating Obavva jayantI on Nov 11 (one day after the purported, but mistaken, Tipu birth day as per Julian calendar). 

Famous picturizations - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tdNjRgW3hBk

c62c548bd5.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in mūlā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°18′37.36″.

c6c2b9dcdf.d: Magnitude: 4% of the solar diameter is covered (parimāṇa ≈0.5 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 17:13►10:23 (from 4 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra uttarāṣāḍhā/śravaṇaḥ/śraviṣṭhā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or rōhiṇī (anujanma) or hastaḥ (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: makaraḥ, kumbhaḥ, mithunam, tulā get more ashubha phala, vr̥ṣabhaḥ, karkaṭaḥ, kanyā, dhanuḥ somewhat ashubha, mīnaḥ, mēṣaḥ, siṁhaḥ, vr̥śchikaḥ shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

c70311a241.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°27′36.48″.
c70311a241.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°27′36.48″, 0°27′25.76″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°36′41.74″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.17, elongation 22°36′41.64″ W). śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°09′05.26″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.93, elongation 22°33′56.04″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c70b75ab55.d:
On this day, the British hung Periya and Chinna Marudhu pANDiyas of shivagangA, tamiL-nADu at Tiruppattur fort.

Context
In 1772, Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah, (the Nawab of Arcot) had killed Muthuvaduganatha Thevar over his refusal to pay taxes. However Marudhu Pandiyars and Queen Velunachiyar escaped, and stayed with Gopala Nayak in Virupakshipuram for 8 years. After this time, an alliance of kingdoms led by the Pandiyar attacked Sivagangai and retook it in 1789. Both Maruthu Pandiyars were given high positions in the kingdom.

After 1781, British took over navAb of Arkot's finances, and then his army. Thence they went from strength to strength. The brothers participated in guerilla war against them. They ultimately captured and hung the marudu brothers.

Aftermath
They are credited with inventing the Valari, a variant of the boomerang; and are honored by local tamils.

c70c8e9109.d:
The Shukla-paksha Ekadashi of vr̥śchikamāsa is also celebrated as kaiśika-ēkādaśī. Kaisika Purāṇam, consisting of 82 shlokas describes the story of nampāḍuvān and a rākṣasa who attained mukti by nāmasaṅkīrtanam and the fruits of nampāḍuvān's nāmasaṅkīrtanam, respectively!

The fruits of fasting on Ekādaśī are greatly extolled in the Padma Purana—

A person who bathes at Śaṃkhoddhāra and beholds the image of Viṣṇu does not acquire even a sixteenth of the merit earned by fasting on Ekādaśī. O noble king, even if one gives four lakhs of coins on the days of the Sun's transition between Zodiac signs, it does not equal even a sixteenth of the merit from an Ekādaśī fast! Indeed, fasting on Ekādaśī grants the same religious merit as bathing at Prabhāsa during a lunar or solar eclipse. One who drinks the sacred water at Kedāra is freed from rebirth, and likewise, fasting on Ekādaśī removes the cycle of rebirth. 

The merit from an Ekādaśī fast is a hundred times greater than the reward of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice on earth. Fasting on Ekādaśī yields a hundredfold more merit than gifting a thousand cows to a learned brāhmaṇa. Those who fast on Ekādaśī are considered equal to those whose bodies are inhabited by Brahma, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The merit from observing the Ekādaśī vow is immeasurable, and difficult to obtain even by the Devas. There is no other vow like that of the Ekādaśī, that destroys sins.
c70c8e9109.s:
𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌪𑍋𑌷𑌣𑌮𑍍।

𑌭𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌰𑍀𑌕𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌮𑍇 𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌦𑌥𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍇 𑌕𑍇𑌶𑌵 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵।  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌵𑍈 𑌵𑌿𑌘𑍍𑌨𑍋 𑌨 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌤𑌃॥  
--𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇  
  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌸𑍌𑌤𑌿𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌪𑌦𑍇𑌶𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌂𑌶𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌨𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌂 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇।  
𑌸 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈𑌕𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑍈 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌵𑌯𑌃॥௧௪॥  
  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇---  
𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌗𑌦𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍॥௩௫॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌨𑍃𑌪𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮॥௩௬॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌷𑍋𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌣𑍇 𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃॥௩௭॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌕𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌰𑍇 𑌚𑍋𑌦𑌕𑌂 𑌪𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௩௮॥  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥 𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌭𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑍀।  
𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍃𑌥𑌿𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௩௯॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍋 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃॥௪௦॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑍂𑌨𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌗𑍋𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌗𑍇॥௪௧॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌤𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌯𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌹𑍇 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌃॥௪௨॥  
𑌵𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌤𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌪𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍋 𑌯𑍇 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌕𑌾𑌃॥௪௩॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌨 𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍈𑌰𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌭𑌮𑍍॥௪௪॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌸𑌮𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௧௮॥  
---𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌶𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌉𑌮𑌾𑌮𑌹𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰𑌸𑌂𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍇 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿-𑌮𑍁𑌰𑌵𑌧𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌚𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌂𑌶𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃॥௪௦॥

c72247c97c.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈3.2 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
c72247c97c.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.27 (parimāṇa ≈3.2 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:31►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

c72cc8c977.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in puṣyaḥ karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′11.02″.
c72cc8c977.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′11.02″, 0°32′52.87″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 0°29′57.03″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.79, elongation 12°31′24.62″ W). budhaḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°03′08.05″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.26, elongation 12°33′25.98″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

c7bdbb9478.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.95″.
c7bdbb9478.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.95″, 0°10′19.13″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′02.64″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′33.54″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′36.69″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′52.85″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c8502cac67.d:
Sāyana-ṣaḍaśīti-puṇyakāla. For ṣaḍaśīti-puṇyakāla, the 60 ghatikas succeeding the saṅkramaṇa form a puṇyakāla; in general, the ghatikas closer to the puṇyakāla are even more sacred.

While the nirayana puṇyakāla-s are well known, marked by the transit of the Sun into various rāśī-s (which confer the name to the corresponding saura month), there are also ayana-s and sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s, which mark the position of the Sun above the Northern or Southern parts of the Earth. These determine the r̥tu-s, and also the very famous uttarāyaṇa and dakṣināyana (movement of the Sun towards North or South, respectively). While these two types of puṇyakāla-s (sāyana and nirayana) coincided millennia ago, there has been a gradual precession of the equinoxes, owing to the nature of the Earth's rotation, causing the sāyana saṅkramaṇa-s to happen about 24 days before the nirayana saṅkramaṇa-s. In that era, uttarāyaṇa coincided with makara-saṅkramaṇa and dakṣināyana coincided with karkaṭaka-saṅkramaṇa, and the mēsa and tulā saṅkramaṇa-s corresponded to the equinoxes, when the Sun rises direct East (and sets direct West).

Many Dharma Shastra texts recognise the separate puṇyakāla-s for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. The vachanam of Jaabaali Maharshi is mentioned above, where he says that the puṇyakāla-s are identical (in their reckoning) for both types of saṅkramaṇa-s. In the Pulastya Siddhanta, the anushthanas which are to be performed in this sayana punya kala just like nirayana are explicitly stated: snāna, dāna, japa, śrāddha, vrata, hōma, etc. In Kala Madhava, which is considered as the source text of the kala vicharas of the Dikshitiya, it is said in the 5th prakarana that,  meṣādi-saṅkrāntayo yasmin dine bhavanti tasmād dināt pūrvebhyaḥ ekādaśabhyo dinebhyaḥ prācīne dine, noting that Sayana Sankramanas occurred ~11 days before the day when the Mesha Sankramanas etc occur. Further references are seen in Dharma Sindhu first pariccheda, Jayasimha Kalpadruma sankranti nirnaya and Nirnaya Sindhu first pariccheda. There are also ample references in Vedas, illustrating how Ayana-s happened much later (in certain other eras), e.g. Shukla Yajur Veda Shatapatha Brahmana (Ekapaat Kanda 1/2/3), Nakshatra Sukta belonging to the Atharva Veda (Shaunaka Samhita 19/7/2), Maitrayaniya Aranyaka (6/14), and Taittiriya Brahmana (1/5/2).

For a wonderfully detailed exposition on the topic, see https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/dakshinayana-en and https://sites.google.com/view/nakshatradarsha/uttarayana-en .
c8502cac67.s:
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌕𑌰𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌶𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌤𑌪𑌃—  
𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌣𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍁 𑌰𑍋𑌗𑍀 𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍁𑌃𑌖𑌭𑌾𑌗𑍀 𑌚 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌹𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌃 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌸𑍁 𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌆𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌕-𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 (𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌃)  
𑌷𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍁𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍇।  
𑌦𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌨𑍈𑌵 𑌦𑍃𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥  
---𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍌𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌭𑍇  
𑌷𑌡𑌶𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌤𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌷𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌿𑌰𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌨𑌾𑌡𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌨𑌾𑌡𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌮𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
---𑌵𑍈𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌥-𑌦𑍀𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑍇 𑌆𑌹𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌕-𑌕𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 (𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌃)  
𑌜𑌾𑌬𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌃---  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑍀𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌯𑌨𑍇 𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌪𑍁𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯-𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇---  
𑌅𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌂𑌶-𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍋 𑌭𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌃 𑌨𑌾𑌲𑍇 𑌚𑌰𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑌾।

c8594cd3c3.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°57′44.58″.
c8594cd3c3.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°57′44.58″, 0°57′40.28″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 0°59′14.33″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 2°22′21.73″ W). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-2 makaraḥ (latitude 1°56′58.91″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.24, elongation 2°54′26.25″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c873bb966e.d:
The Adhikara Nandi festival a special day within the larger Panguni Utsavam, the 10-day annual festival celebrated at the Sri Kapaleeshwarar Temple in Mylapore, Chennai. The festival celebrates the divine bull Nandi, the mount of Bhagavan Shiva. [Image of Nandi, the mount of Bhagavan Shiva]
Adhigara translates to "Supreme Bull" or "King of Bulls", highlighting Nandi's importance as Shiva's loyal companion and vahanam.

On the morning of the third day of the Panguni Utsavam, Bhagavan Kapaleeshwarar, the presiding deity of the temple, is adorned in special ornaments and taken out in a procession mounted on a silver-plated Nandi. The procession winds through the "Mada" streets of Mylapore, accompanied by devotional music, chants, and enthusiastic devotees.

The sight of the majestic silver Nandi adorned with flowers and jewels, carrying Bhagavan Kapaleeshwarar, is a mesmerising spectacle. Devotees throng the streets to witness the procession, shower blessings, and participate in the joyous celebrations. The procession culminates in the temple complex, where special rituals and pujas are performed for Bhagavan Kapaleeshwarar and Nandi.

c885af6af3.b: Observed on Śukla-Pañcamī tithi of Caitraḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
c885af6af3.d: Celebrating the birth of uchchaiśravā horse, offer puja to horses or even Bhagavan Hayagriva.
c885af6af3.s:
𑌉𑌚𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌃𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌕𑍇।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌰𑌗𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌬𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌵𑌾𑌃।  
𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌕𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌶𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌭𑍀𑌮𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌰𑌥𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌵𑌿𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌵𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍀।  
𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌶𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌶𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌕𑌲𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌹𑌹𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌃।  
𑌸𑍁𑌬𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌰𑌥𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍁𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍇𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌵𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌬𑌦𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌶𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌶𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍀 𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌤𑌿𑌬𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌵𑌸𑍁𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌽𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌃॥  
𑌇𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍈𑌰𑍁𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌵𑌚𑍈𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾।   
𑌮𑍋𑌦𑌕𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌭𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌪𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍈𑌃॥  
𑌦𑌧𑍍𑌨𑌾 𑌗𑍁𑌡𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑌯𑌸𑌾 𑌶𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌪𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍇𑌨 𑌭𑍂𑌰𑌿𑌶𑌃।  
𑌧𑍂𑌪𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌦𑍀𑌪𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌚𑌨𑍈𑌃॥  
𑌏𑌵𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍 𑌤𑍁𑌰𑌗𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌬𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌵𑌾𑌃।  
𑌬𑌲𑌮𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌜𑌯𑌮𑍍॥

c8ad580355.d:
On this day, Skardu was lost to betrayal by muslim-dominated Gilgit Scouts.

Context
With the betrayal at Gilgit, the command of 6 J&K Infantry now devolved on Major Sher Jung Thapa. Skardu was east of Gilgit and an important town. 6 J&K infantry, was spread out thinly in penny packets from Leh to Bunji. Capt Ganga Singh commanded two platoons at Kargil, which entirely comprised of Sikhs. Skardu itself was held by two platoons under Capt Nek Alam with entirely Muslim soldiers. 

Thapa was at Leh when Gilgit fell and he was ordered to March to Skardu with whatever troops available. He arrived there on 3rd December and immediately noticed the hostile environment. He sought permission to withdraw the garrison and the civil administration to Kargil and also requested reinforcements. The request for withdrawal was turned down and he was asked "to hold to last man and last round". Gilgit Scouts and raiders were moving towards Skardu. By mid-February, Skardu received some small reinforcements from Srinagar.

Thapa had 130 non-Muslim and 31 Muslim troops in Skardu now. He had deployed Nek Alam and his Muslim platoon 32 km towards west, on the road from Gilgit, which followed the river. Another platoon of Sikhs was positioned on the other bank of the river. This was at a place called Tsari. By the start of February, tribesmen and the traitors from 6 J&K Infantry had completed all the plans to capture Skardu. 

On the 9th of February, the enemies attacked. Nek Alam and his soldiers immediately changed sides. Krishna Singh and his small platoon were routed and the survivors murdered in cold blood.

They then moved towards Skardu, while Thapa was unaware of the disaster and treachery at Tsari. The first attack by raiders on 11th February was beaten back while some Muslims of Thapa’s garrison deserted. Skardu also received some more reinforcements and now had 285 soldiers. Thapa also provided shelter to all the non-Muslims of the town, which numbered around 229.  Indian Army, assembled 3 successive Skardu relief columns, but they were not successful in reaching Skardu. Air-dropping of ammunition was also not effective.

Skardu was besieged by well-armed raiders and Muslim troops, while Thapa defended it gallantly till August 14. They had fought without adequate ammunition, food, or even water. Finally, Skardu capitulated, outnumbered five to one, and with the last box of the reserve ammunition used. 

Aftermath
All the surviving non-Muslims were murdered, but their women abducted, raped, and sold into brothels. Major Thapa and his orderly were the only ones kept alive. He was returned to Bharat some days after the war and was awarded Mahavir Chakra.

c8cf801b6a.d: Tiruvaḷḷuva Nayanmar (or Tiruvaḷḷuvar) was born in Vaikasi month, Anuradha nakshatram. A veritable sage, he gave the world a "threefold speech" embodying dharma, artha, kāma, and who taught the eternal Sanātana dharma in a manner not contradicting the Vedas and Āgamas. The Tirukkuṟaḷ is a work of 1,330 couplets arranged in 133 chapters of ten couplets each. It is organized into three sections — aṟam, poruḷ, inbam. These correspond directly to three of the four Sanskrit puruṣārthas: dharma, artha, kāma. Tiruvaḷḷuvar is typically depicted (in older texts) with a tripuṇḍra (vibhūti marking) on the forehead and rudrākṣa beads — along with matted hair (jaṭā), the cin-mudrā, a seated ascetic posture, and disciples nearby, typical of sages/Rishis.
c8cf801b6a.s:

c8df44221b.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′15.78″.
c8df44221b.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°36′15.78″, 0°36′02.36″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°15′32.11″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.71, elongation 25°42′15.54″ W). śukraḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°39′16.34″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.87, elongation 25°39′41.05″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

c96de6ae74.b: Event occured on 1660-07-23 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
c96de6ae74.d:
It was AshADha k1 (as per jedhe shAkhAvali). bAji prabhu deshpANDe (a kAyastha) leading ~300 men died holding back Adil-shAhi african general siddi masud's 10k soldiers in a narrow pass while shivAji leading his 300 escaped from panhaLa fort to the beseiged vishAlgad fort (some say he sent out a decoy - Shiva Kashid- as well).

bAjI prabhu bought him time to escape, holding back the pursuing enemy (under Jauhar's son Siddi Aziz and Afzal Khan's son Fazl Khan) at the gajapur pass (aka ghoD-khiND, later renamed pAvana-khiND to recall bAhI-prabhu's sacrifice). shivAjI, after fighting fiercely (supposedly holding daNDapaTTa swords in both hands) at vishAlgaD surroundings for 5 hours, announced his safe entry into vishAlgaD with cannon-fire. It is said that bAjI only then died with relief.  

PS: vishAlgad was already under siege by Bijapuri sardars under siddi jauhar - Suryarao Surve and Jaswantrao Dalvi. But shivAjI's posse, assisted by that of the brAhmaNa chief rango nArAyaN (attacking from Gonimooth hill), relieved the defenders and routed the attackers upon arrival. It's a thrilling tale, akin to tale of the spartans holding back the persians at the narrow pass at Thermopylae.

Aftermath:  
- bAjI prabhu and most of his men died. Other casualities included his brother Fulaji Prabhu and Shambusing Jadhav. On the sultan's side - 1k to 5k died in both actions.
- Shivaji then safely crossed the western ghats and reached his capital Rajgad via Konkan region.
- Shivaji later personally visited the house of the slain Baji Prabhu and honored and helped his family. It is said that Shivaji’s mother, Jijabai, wept at the news of Baji Prabhu’s death.

c9aa97db0e.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°27′36.96″.
c9aa97db0e.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°27′36.96″, 0°27′26.24″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°36′42.30″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.17, elongation 22°36′42.01″ W). śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°09′05.34″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.93, elongation 22°33′56.37″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
c9aa97db0e.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।
